explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on the little “glue” tokens that structure formal boilerplate—prepositions (“at”), conjunctions (“or”), imperatives in policy or forum instructions (“post,” “continue”) and even block delimiters (“}”)—i.e. the words and symbols that introduce links, choices or section boundaries in legal, documentation and code-header text.
This neuron detects the structural break between a heading/metadata line (titles, bylines, captions, “Read more” links, etc.) and the start of the body text that follows.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires at the very start of new documents or major sections—headlines, bylines, datelines, copyright headers, legal-docket headings, “Produced by” lines, etc. It marks “we’re now at the top of a document/section.”

This neuron fires on standout domain-specific terms and names—those multi-letter tokens (acronyms, technical abbreviations, study or test labels, chemical formulas, proper names or titles) that mark specialized concepts or entities in scientific/academic and news writing.

This neuron seems to fire on words that flag non-factual or “irrealis” discourse—i.e. interrogatives, hypotheticals, speculation or legal/conditional clauses.  It lights up on question markers (Is, Does, How, Where, Why, Can…), hedges (“unlikely,” “however”), quantifiers in counterfactual/legal contexts (“any,” “event” in “in no event shall…”), etc.
This neuron marks the ends of standalone headings or titles (often a final token like a period or last word in a section‐title line) across varied document genres.

This feature lights up on abstract, discourse-level nouns—especially nominalizations—that name states, relations or judgments (e.g. “effect,” “disconnect,” “importance,” “frustration,” “role,” etc.), regardless of the specific topic.

This feature fires on the “preamble” or boilerplate header of a file or document—i.e. the top‐of‐file metadata markers such as comment delimiters (/*…*/), copyright and license lines, publication‐status flags (UNPUBLISHED, NOT PRECEDENTIAL), court header names, package/import directives, etc.

This neuron fires on the little “glue” words and punctuation that set up or highlight a statement’s core predicate—chiefly copulas (is, was, be, ’s) together with their negations or intensifiers (not, literally, now) and even structural markers (colons, chapter‐number tokens) that introduce definitions, explanations or other focal clauses. It’s essentially a “statement‐framing” feature.

This feature fires on the final token (often punctuation or the last word) of a heading/title or headline — in blogs, news articles, lists, etc. — effectively marking the boundary where a title ends and the body text begins.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on clause-introducing function words—complementizers like “that”/“which,” infinitival “to,” and similar subordinators (e.g. in “in turn”) that link a main clause to its subordinate or relative clause.

The feature is essentially a detector for “(” – it lights up at the opening of parenthetical asides or metadata chunks (dates, docket numbers, bylines, locations, credits, etc.) in news-style or legal/formal prose.

This feature fires on short relational prepositions (with, to, of, by) that introduce adjuncts or complements—e.g. marking agents (“written by”), recipients (“email to”), associations (“talk with”) or possessive/partitive links (“names of”) in prose about communication, attribution, or legal/metadata contexts.
This feature is a detector for the double‐asterisk (“**”) markers that delimit bold or emphasized text in Markdown/Wiki‐style formatting.

This feature detects the preposition “of” (and related high-weight tokens like “Appeals”) in formal legal or licensing boilerplate—e.g. in case-heading phrases such as “Court of Appeals” and in license disclaimers like “without warranties or conditions of any kind.”

This neuron fires on the very start of a new “header‐like” block or section—titles, bylines, license‐disclaimer blocks, court-case captions, news headlines, sports headings, etc. In other words, it marks the opening tokens of structured document metadata or section headers across many domains.

This neuron is picking out the “main identifier” in namespaced or punctuated constructs—the first real name token that follows a delimiter (e.g. the scope in “@angular/core” or “@aws‐sdk…,” the value after an HTML/XML attribute’s “=”, or the middle word in a multi-word proper name like “Mary Beth Kelly”).

This neuron lights up on the final token of a headline, title or section label—whether it’s the last word (often a proper name or key term) or the closing punctuation (period, abbreviation) in news‐style headings, sports divisions, show/episode titles, etc. It thus marks the boundary at the end of a formatted headline or title across varied contexts.

This neuron fires on line- or sentence-initial tokens that serve as discourse or structural markers—e.g. temporal adverbs (“Recent,” “Earlier,” “Given,” “When,” “As”), functional heads (“Evidence,” “Respond,” “Molecular”), dates (“2013,” “2001”), or topic-introducing proper nouns (“Davis,” “Journalist,” “Human”)—essentially flagging the start of new sections or clauses.
This feature detects hyphenation marks—i.e. the “‐” or related dash characters used to join or break words into compounds (half-time, self-compassion, min-width, soft-hyphens, etc.).

This neuron spot‐lights the “end of a headline/label” boundary in web text. It consistently fires on the final token (often a period or label like “News,” “Inc.”, etc.) that closes off a title or section header and signals the start of the main body.

This neuron is essentially a little “two-character chunk” detector: it fires on recurring bi-grams or subword glimpses that signal common structural affixes or notation markers across domains—e.g. the “^{” of LaTeX exponents, doubled-letter caps like LL, SP, IC in code or legal IDs, the Japanese long-vowel/‐tari suffix (ッタリ), the Hebrew v-prefix (ו-), Russian suffix bits (ож, в), the Japanese ーコード (“-code”), Thai script glyphs, etc. In short, it flags frequent two-char patterns that mark domain-specific morphological or syntactic units.
This feature marks sentence-boundary positions, firing strongly on the final token of a sentence (often the last word or the closing punctuation).

This neuron seems to fire on standalone “identifier” tokens in two guises:  
– Four-digit numerals used as calendar years or timestamps in prose or metadata (e.g. 2013, 1967, 2016, 1940, etc.)  
– Single-letter symbols naming the unknown in algebraic equations (e.g. x, n, s, q, l, o, i)

This neuron appears to flag in-text reference/citation markers (e.g. “[@CR1]”, “^[@bibr1…]”, “CIT0001”, etc.) and similar bibliographic cross-reference tokens commonly found in academic or technical documents.

This neuron fires on the little “boilerplate” or header markers that kick off a new section in all kinds of text or code—datelines and PRNewswire leads, patent “Field of the Invention” headings, UMD-module wrappers in JavaScript, section titles (e.g. “Access to documents — Regulation EC ...”), journal-style citations and references (e.g. “Fischhoff et al. (1987)”), chemical article titles or scheme numbers, grant acknowledgments (NIH/CRISP), cytogenetic loci, etc.—i.e. tokens that signal the start of a formal, highly structured block.

This neuron fires on clause-initial verbs that introduce facilitation or linkage—words like “allow,” “using,” “connecting,” “put,” “blended,” etc.—i.e. discourse markers that signal how one element enables, links, or brings about another in the text.

This neuron fires on domain-specific “label” tokens—the little abbreviation- or classification-style words you see in scientific/medical (and even code) text.  Examples include chemical symbols (Zn), lipid or protein acronyms (LDL), virus abbreviations (HBV, HSV), axis labels (Y), scoring names (Gleason), subtype markers (squamous cell), cytokine types (Th2), etc.

This neuron fires on the final token of section titles or headings (e.g. the last word or symbol at the end of blog‐post titles, menu labels, code‐doc headers, etc.), effectively marking the boundary where a heading line ends.

This neuron is basically a sub-word “affix” detector that lights up on the little chunks you see in organic-chemistry names (amino-, ‑ol, ‑ylic, ‑ros-, ‑ocy-, dihydro-, etc.). In other domains it still fires on the same BPE pieces (e.g. two-letter blocks, numbers or hyphens in IDs), but its highest activations are on those characteristic chemical functional-group suffixes.

This feature detects high-level section or UI labels in text—things like headings, menu/navigation markers, article titles and other structural labels (e.g. “Video:”, “Post Top Ad”, “Main menu”, “News”, “Hidden Answers”, “Post navigation”, etc.).
This feature detects in-text academic citation markers (the “[@…]” or “[CR…]”‐style bibliography references) typical of scientific paper introductions.
This feature detects the very start of a multi-line source-code comment that holds copyright/license boilerplate (e.g. the leading “/*” of an Apache, GPL, MIT, etc. header).

This neuron is a “discourse‐marker” detector: it lights up on the little tokens that signal informal or conversational phrasing—contractions and ’s (don’t, that’s, it’s), trailing ellipses (…), and short action or stance words (tap, burn, decrypt/crypt, am, great) that typically occur in quoted speech, imperatives or procedural/instructional passages. It thus flags the bits of text that carry the speaker’s or writer’s conversational tone and structural cues.

This neuron is a generic “heading/title” detector: it spikes on front-matter labels and section headers (e.g. menu labels, blog or news headlines, API comment titles, service or company section names, scientific article titles, etc.) across diverse text domains.

explanations.explanation: This feature detects subword fragments containing unusual or marked characters—e.g. diacritics (ô, é, ú), Scandinavian ø, Cyrillic щ/ж, uppercase Base64 digrams, chemical prefixes (“glut-,” “ox-”) or the English “year-” in age expressions—i.e. orthographically distinctive chunks that signal foreign-language spellings or technical terms.
